title: ICC Members Vote to Dismiss Prosecutor Karim Khan Over Sexual Misconduct Allegations
excerpt: Eighty-two of the International Criminal Court's 125 member states voted to remove the British-Pakistani barrister in a secret ballot at UN headquarters in New York.
body:
• ICC member states voted 82-43 on Friday to dismiss chief prosecutor Karim Khan over sexual misconduct allegations, exceeding the 63-vote threshold required for removal.
  • Khan, 56, a British-Pakistani barrister, denies all wrongdoing and has called the process unlawful and procedurally unfair.
  • The dismissal comes as the US has sanctioned 11 ICC officials and launched a diplomatic campaign to dismantle the court.
  • Khan made global headlines in 2024 by seeking arrest warrants for Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu over the Gaza conflict.

Member states of the International Criminal Court voted on Friday to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor, ending an 18-month crisis that has shaken the world's permanent war crimes tribunal at a time when it faces an unprecedented campaign by the United States to dismantle it.

Eighty-two of the court's 125 member states voted in favour of Khan's removal in a secret ballot held at United Nations headquarters in New York, well above the absolute majority of 63 required, according to two diplomatic sources who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.

The Allegations

Khan's removal follows allegations of sexual misconduct by a junior ICC staff member identified only by her first name, Sarah. A Malaysian Muslim lawyer in her late thirties, she alleged that Khan sexually harassed her and subjected her to non-consensual sexual acts during work trips, including an incident in a hotel room in Colombia.

https://x.com/KenRoth/status/2080704856395043227

In an interview with CNN's Christiane Amanpour earlier this month — her first public appearance — Sarah described feeling "humiliated" and pointed to the power disparity between herself and the prosecutor. "There is no way for something to be consensual when you have such a power disparity," she said.

Khan, 56, has cooperated with the UN investigation but categorically denies any wrongdoing. His legal team has called the process that led to the vote "unlawful, procedurally unfair and unsupported by evidence."

"The court is already in a precarious state. The Khan situation is a separate but very significant part of the overall perception of the court's credibility."

— Mark Ellis, Executive Director, International Bar Association

A Prosecutor Who Challenged World Powers

Born in Edinburgh to a Pakistani dermatologist and a British nurse, Khan studied law in London before building a career at the intersection of international criminal justice and geopolitics. He served as legal adviser for UN war crimes tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda before winning the ICC prosecutor role in 2021 after intense lobbying by the UK and African states.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ac8HNq8TL18

Khan thrust the ICC into a direct confrontation with Washington in May 2024 when he sought arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over the Gaza conflict. The move drew fierce US opposition and contributed to the sanctions campaign that now targets 11 of the court's top officials.

In 2023, the court also issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin, which resulted in Khan being convicted in a 2025 in-absentia trial in Russia.

US Campaign Against the ICC

Khan's dismissal lands amid an escalating US effort to dismantle the court. Just last week, Washington announced a renewed diplomatic campaign against the ICC, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declaring during a visit to the Philippines that there were "lunatics and crazies involved in the ICC."

The US, which is not an ICC member state, has said no diplomatic options are off the table. President Trump and other US officials have long maintained that the court should not have authority to investigate or prosecute Americans.

What Comes Next

The ICC will need to select a new chief prosecutor, a process that could take months and will unfold against the backdrop of US pressure and internal divisions among member states. The court's credibility — already strained by the Khan allegations and the US sanctions — will depend on whether its next leader can restore confidence in its independence and mandate.

For the broader South Asian legal community, Khan's rise and fall represents both the remarkable reach of diaspora professionals into global institutions and the intense scrutiny that comes with such positions.
